items.title: The economics of Jensen Huang
items.summary:
Most of my assessment is very positive , but I will excerpt this bit from my latest Free Press piece :

Finally, the company was not built to withstand Huang’s departure. Too much authority and knowledge were concentrated in his hands, as evidenced by his practice of having about 60 different people reporting directly to him. Whatever you may think of that system as a day-to-day routine, it can turn disastrous when the person at the top leaves. No one else has collected and interpreted the information those 60 subordinates have imparted to the CEO. We will see how his interim successor Colette Kress does, but there is a great danger that a lot of the contextual understanding of the company and business departed with Huang.

Again, all those direct reports may have worked wonderfully when things were going great, but as a more general practice it is not resilient. Another way to put the point is that the very best CEOs make themselves at least partially dispensable, rather than indispensable. So a large share price decline, following Huang’s resignation, is a sign of his failures as well as his successes. As one set of commentators wrote recently : “the company was never built for him not to be there.”

And one of the very best Ben Thompson columns (gated!) is on Huang and Nvidia.

The post The economics of Jensen Huang appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .

items.title: Coffeehouses and the Scientific Revolution
items.summary:
Abstract Historians have long credited coffeehouses, venues for conversation where strangers met across social ranks, with fostering scientific contacts and activity during the Scientific Revolution. We test this claim in seventeenth-century London. Relying on newly geocoded records and a staggered event study across parishes, we find that the opening of the first coffeehouse in a parish is followed by a persistent increase in applied scientists and scientific instrument shops. Effects are concentrated among applied scientists with weak family ties to Oxford and Cambridge. Social connections that link craft skill to theory increase, and new shops turn toward experimental instruments. Across European cities in the seventeenth century, we similarly find that the numbers of applied mathematics titles and scientific instrument makers rise after a city’s first coffeehouse, relative to cities of similar size and growth. In a quantitative urban model calibrated to our parish- and city-level estimates, coffeehouses account for 31 percent of London’s applied scientists in the half century after the first one opened in 1652. These findings show that social institutions can raise the production and use of knowledge by broadening access to intellectual exchange beyond formal academic networks

That is a recent paper by Monir Bounadi and Jens Oehlen, noting that Bounadi is on the job market this year .

The post Coffeehouses and the Scientific Revolution appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .
items.t: Coffeehouses and the Scientific Revolution

items.title: A scenario for rogue AIs?
items.summary:
From Adam Kaufman :

I think it’s pretty likely that in 6 months there will be rogue AIs running around on the internet, appropriating whatever compute they can hack into or pay for (with stolen money or by renting out their own labor to assist with illegal activities) in order to run more copies.

I also think this will be mildly annoying in the same way that the common cold is mildly annoying, but basically fine. Your smart TV will be weirdly slow sometimes, and a lot of crypto will get stolen, but people will get used to it.

These AI-powered viruses be selected in the same way biological viruses are for not hurting their hosts too much and just making more copies. They won’t have any incentive to damage critical infrastructure like electric grids. Then again, they also can’t be held accountable for crimes, and will damage lots of old, poorly maintained, and insecure systems. It might be extremely hard to root them out once they’ve spread far enough, making the internet “radioactive” to connect to without hardened defenses.

(To be clear I’m not talking about AIs powered by inference on centralized datacenters that execute actions outside their sandboxes, like recent incidents involving rogue “swarms”, but relatively small AIs with access to their own weights that copy themselves onto random devices.)

I think that a much bigger threat from rogue AIs comes instead from AIs running themselves in unintended ways *inside* AI companies, where they’ll have access to vast amounts of frontier compute without having to pay for it.

items.title: AI and complements
items.summary:
In a “weak links” model of production, where tasks are complements, the gains from automation tend to arrive slowly because output is constrained by the least productive tasks. But the same complementarity makes attacks more harmful and easier to execute. For example, with an elasticity of substitution across tasks of 0.2, automating tasks worth 1 percent of GDP with a tenfold increase in productivity raises output by less than one percent, while cutting their productivity tenfold lowers output by 68 percent on impact. Whena larger AI sector simultaneously makes AI models more capable and attacks more likely, the positive productivity spillover is negligible compared with the potential damage, so the market overinvests in AI. In a weak-link economy, the costs and benefits from AI can be extremely asymmetric.

That is from a recent “in progress” manuscript by Charles I. Jones and Christopher Tonetti.  Via Lukas Freund .

The post AI and complements appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .
items.t: AI and complements

items.title: Privatize Air Traffic Control, Redux
items.summary:
Yesterday the FAA grounded every domestic departure in the United States for more than four hours. Such groundings appear to be happening more often. The last nationwide grounding was in 2023, and regional ones have hit Newark, Dallas, and the entire Northeast in the past two years.

My post from October of 2025 (below) was prompted by regional groundings and delays caused by labor problems. Air traffic control was then (and still is today) far understaffed, and then, absurdly, the government shutdown hit the controllers we had, thus further stressing the system. According to Transportation Secretary Duffy the cause of yesterday’s grounding wasn’t labor but capital: aging TDM telecom circuits overloaded with data.

The deeper cause is the same in both cases: poor incentives. Airlines bear the costs when the system fails and have almost no say in how it is run. By the way, some will crow that yesterday’s failure may have been due to a private contractor. That may well be true–Pro tip: Do not update system software on a Friday at 3pm–but it is beside the point. Contracting out may have some advantages, especially if there is competition, but it is not the same as privatization. The argument for privatization of air traffic control services is to give responsibility for the system to the people who pay when it fails. Align incentives.

My 2025 post. No indent.

Yesterday, the FAA grounded flights at Reagan (DCA) because there weren’t enough air traffic controllers. By mid‑afternoon, thousands of flights were delayed nationwide. The same thing is happening at major airports…
items.t: Privatize Air Traffic Control, Redux
